identity_evidence.quote: A 35-year-old woman with end-stage renal disease secondary to IgA nephropathy underwent a living donor kidney transplantation at 33 years of age, with her mother serving as the donor

fields.chief_complaint: Recurrent febrile urinary tract infection/acute pyelonephritis of transplanted kidney

evidence.quote: A 35-year-old woman with end-stage renal disease secondary to IgA nephropathy underwent a living donor kidney transplantation at 33 years of age, with her mother serving as the donor. Her bilateral native kidneys had not been removed and remained in situ. The donor’s left kidney was implanted in the recipient’s right iliac fossa, with end-to-side anastomoses of the renal artery and vein to the external iliac artery and vein. An extravesical ureteroneocystostomy was performed according to the Lich-Gregoir technique with creation of a submucosal tunnel to provide an anti-reflux mechanism. The early postoperative course was uneventful, and graft function stabilized with a serum creatinine level of approximately 1.2 mg/dL (reference range for adult women in our laboratory: 0.46-0.79 mg/dL).

At one year and one month after transplantation, she developed her first episode of fUTI consistent with acute pyelonephritis of the transplanted kidney, which resolved with intravenous followed by oral antibiotics. Thereafter, she experienced multiple recurrent episodes of acute pyelonephritis despite the introduction of prophylactic antibiotics. During this period, repeated fUTIs and infection-related dehydration led to a transient deterioration of graft function, with the serum creatinine level rising from a baseline of approximately 1.2 mg/dL to a maximum of 3.30 mg/dL. This pattern of recurrent febrile infection and transient graft dysfunction prompted further evaluation for an anatomic cause.
Two years and six months after kidney transplantation, she was admitted for endoscopic correction of vesicoureteral reflux

facts.clinical_statement: Adult female living-donor transplant recipient with recurrent febrile allograft infection

time.text: Over 52 months of follow-up after Deflux injection

evidence.quote: Over 52 months of follow-up after Deflux injection, our patient experienced no further episodes of acute pyelonephritis and maintained serum creatinine at approximately 1.2 mg/dL. Compared with previously published series, the present case illustrates several clinically relevant points. First, the patient was a relatively young adult with a living donor renal allograft and recurrent febrile pyelonephritis despite prophylactic antibiotics, representing a scenario in which both infection control and graft preservation are crucial. Second, Deflux injection using a double-HIT-based technique achieved durable elimination of VUR and infections without the need for open reimplantation, thus controlling symptoms while avoiding the additional morbidity and vascular risk associated with repeat pelvic surgery.

facts.clinical_statement: Durable VUR resolution in long-term follow-up

summary.text: A 35-year-old woman with end-stage renal disease from IgA nephropathy underwent living-donor kidney transplantation at age 33, with her mother as donor. The donor’s left kidney was implanted in the recipient’s right iliac fossa with end-to-side vascular anastomoses and Lich-Gregoir extravesical ureteroneocystostomy. Both native kidneys remained in situ. Early recovery was uneventful, with graft function stabilized at serum creatinine approximately 1.2mg/dL.

First febrile allograft pyelonephritis occurred 13months after transplantation and resolved with intravenous followed by oral antibiotics. Multiple episodes recurred despite prophylaxis, with infection-related dehydration and transient graft dysfunction; creatinine peaked at 3.30mg/dL. VCUG showed grade II allograft VUR, clinically significant despite low grade. A small previously uremic bladder was presumed, not measured.

After discussing conservative prophylaxis and surgical/endoscopic options, she elected endoscopic correction 30months after transplantation. Under spinal anesthesia, cystoscopy identified a mildly dilated orifice on the right anterior bladder wall. Temporary ureteral stent alignment and a metallic needle facilitated double-HIT submucosal Deflux injection of 2mL. A satisfactory mound and slit-like orifice formed without intraoperative complications. The urethral catheter was removed on postoperative day 1 and she was discharged on day 2.

VCUG three months after injection showed complete VUR resolution. At 52months, no further pyelonephritis or febrile UTI occurred; serial urinalyses and cultures remained negative without asymptomatic bacteriuria. Creatinine improved to 1.18mg/dL, near pre-infection baseline, with stable graft function and no obstruction, hydronephrosis or procedure complications. Open reimplantation was unnecessary. The creatinine values are retained without calling them normal against the local reference interval.
